newsitem.title: ISRAEL: ISRAELI CPI-LINKED BONDS END LOWER.
newsitem.headline: ISRAELI CPI-LINKED BONDS END LOWER.

text.p: Israeli unlinked bonds closed higher on Monday while prices of CPI-linked bonds fell in what traders said was a continuation of a technical correction.
* Bank of Israel short-term Makam bills: +0.03 pct to 108.6
Volume including Makams was an average 153 million shekels.

"Trading today was a continuation and even a strengthening of a trend started in the last few trading days. Prices of all kinds of unlinked bonds rose slightly today, while prices of CPI-linked bonds fell across the board," said Ofer Agassi of the Financial Immunities consulting firm.

"CPI-linked bonds made a very big move in the last two months, with yields falling on average from 4.2 percent two months ago to 3.6 percent. Yields on long bonds are at 3.7 percent. This trend stopped about three days ago and now yields are rising slightly on a technical correction," Agassi said.

He said prices of unlinked bonds were higher despite expectations of a high July consumer price index (CPI). "Traders are looking forward and not just at the coming CPIs. Players believe that in the next 12 months inflation will be within its target," Agassi said.

The rise of the dollar against the shekel in June, which caused June's CPI to rise a steep 1.1 percent, has triggered fears of a series of high indices in the coming months. July's CPI, to published on Friday, is feared to be a high one to 1.2 percent.

"The government issued today 500 million shekels worth of 15-year, fixed-interest CPI-linked bonds and prices closed at one percent below the market price," said a trader at a major institutional investor.
"The issue was sold very cheaply and could trigger a further fall in prices of CPI-linked bonds," the trader said.
Prices of dollar-linked bonds were stable, Agassi said.
The Tel Aviv Stock Exchange will be closed on Tuesday because of the Jewish fast day of Tisha B'Av.
Note: Makams are zero-coupon unlinked certificates with durations of three months to one year. The Bank of Israel issues Makams to absorb liquidity.
